strengths: Strong empirical results achieving SOTA single-step generation with 100x RTF speedup over diffusion baselines on multiple metrics (FAD, FD, KL, IS, CLAP)
Well-motivated instantaneous-to-mean curriculum with flow field mix-up that is thoroughly validated through ablation studies showing necessity of each component
Clever integration of classifier-free guidance into training targets to eliminate inference overhead without compromising quality
Comprehensive experimental validation with multiple datasets (884k samples) and thorough ablations (Tables 2-4) demonstrating training stability
Practical advantages: lightweight 120M parameter model trainable on consumer GPUs in 3 days, self-contained without requiring teacher models
Clear technical presentation with sound mathematical formulation and well-structured algorithmic descriptions
Good reproducibility with detailed implementation details and promised open-sourcing of code and weights
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: applies MeanFlow from concurrent work (Geng et al. 2025) in relatively straightforward manner; main novel contributions (curriculum, CFG integration) are incremental engineering contributions

Evaluation fairness concerns: models compared with different training data amounts/sources, different text encoders, and inconsistent CFG integration status (Table 1 footnotes); marginal speedup over ConsistencyTTA (0.013 vs 0.017 RTF) undermines '100x' claim
Lack of human evaluation: relies solely on automated metrics without listening tests or qualitative audio comparisons; no validation that generated audio is perceptually better

CFG integration insufficiently analyzed: claim that training-time guidance achieves equivalent inference-time guidance lacks theoretical justification or empirical validation; effective scale formula assumes equivalence without proof

Training curriculum requires manual dataset quality designation and hyperparameter tuning (75% flow mix-up ratio); instability at 0% and 25% ratios (Table 3) suggests fragility; limited guidance for domain transfer
Architectural contributions not ablated: heavy borrowing from Flux (MMDiT, DiT blocks, ConvMLP, RoPE, RMSNorm) without isolating their contributions from MeanFlow itself
Abstract inconsistency (RTF stated as 0.013 vs 0.016 in text); multi-step generation claims ('smooth and coherent transitions') unvalidated; limited failure case analysis

Questionable design choices lack justification: hyperparameters (ω=0.3, κ=0.9, logit-normal μ=0.4/σ=1), batch size difference between stages, hidden dimension 448, block counts N1=4/N2=8 appear arbitrary

strengths: Strong empirical results on automatic metrics (FAD, FD, KL improvements of 23.3%, 22.2%, 7.7% respectively) with impressive 100x speedup and single-step generation quality
Practical and efficient: trainable in 3 days on consumer RTX 3090 GPUs with only 120M parameters, addressing real deployment constraints
Comprehensive ablation studies rigorously validating each component (curriculum, flow mix-up, CFG), with clear methodology and experimental design
Clever integration of classifier-free guidance into training target to eliminate inference overhead, avoiding the standard 2x cost
Sound technical execution with correct mathematics and reasonable experimental methodology overall
weaknesses: Severely limited novelty: primarily applies existing MeanFlow technique (Geng et al. 2025) to audio without methodological innovation. Main novel contribution is a straightforward two-stage curriculum lacking theoretical justification or principled design

Critical absence of human evaluation—entirely missing for audio generation task. Automatic metrics alone cannot assess audio quality, naturalness, or prompt adherence as perceived by humans, representing a fundamental gap for generation work

Evaluation scope too narrow: only AudioCaps test set (957 samples) with no evaluation on other datasets, out-of-distribution samples, or analysis of failure modes; no investigation of which audio types the model handles well or poorly
Reproducibility issues: code and model weights not provided despite promises; implementation details insufficient (VAE architecture, pretraining specifications); blank URLs for project and code links

No qualitative analysis whatsoever: no audio samples, spectrograms, visualizations of learned representations across training stages, or sample comparisons with baselines; impossible to assess quality beyond metrics

Limited NLP contribution unsuitable for ACL: text encoding uses existing models (CLAP, FLAN-T5) with no novel NLP methodology; paper is fundamentally an audio generation application better suited to audio/multimedia venues (ICASSP, InterSpeech, ICLR)

Insufficient justification for design choices: hyperparameters (ω=0.3, κ=0.9, 75% mix-up ratio) appear empirically motivated without exploration; no analysis of alternatives or sensitivity studies; missing discussion of failure modes, maximum audio lengths, or limitations

strengths: Strong empirical results: achieves SOTA single-step TTA (FAD 1.77, FD 15.40) with 100x speedup and only 120M parameters compared to 500M+ competitors

Well-motivated technical solutions: integrated CFG eliminates sampling overhead; instantaneous-to-mean curriculum directly solves identified training instability issues; thoughtful architectural choices (ConvMLP, RoPE, RMSNorm)

Comprehensive experimental validation: detailed ablation studies convincingly demonstrate necessity of each component; curriculum ablation shows clear improvements over baselines; flow mix-up ratio and CFG scale analysis provide insights
High reproducibility: clear algorithm descriptions, detailed hyperparameters, promised code release; implementation details enable reproduction
First application of MeanFlow to text-to-audio generation, opening a new direction for efficient TTA; addresses real problem of slow inference in practical applications
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: MeanFlow framework and integrated CFG approach are from concurrent work (Geng et al. 2025); main contribution is training curriculum, which while useful is relatively incremental; architecture uses standard components

Critical gap: no human perceptual evaluation or listening studies reported; automatic metrics (FAD, FD, IS, KL, CLAP) don't capture actual user experience; for 1-step generation quality to be validated, human preference studies are essential

Practical applicability unclear: single-step generation may have perceptible quality degradation; users needing acceptable quality would require multi-step inference, significantly reducing speedup advantage; no analysis of quality-speed trade-off boundaries

Limited evaluation scope: only AudioCaps test set; no validation on Clotho despite training inclusion; cross-domain generalization (music, speech, other sound types) not explored; fixed to 10-second audio; failure case analysis absent

Unaddressed technical details: JVP computation adds training overhead (not quantified); stop-gradient operation insufficiently justified; CFG parameters (ω=0.3, κ=0.9) and flow ratio (75%) appear empirically tuned without principled justification; two-stage curriculum adds complexity without single-stage alternative analysis

Speedup claims require qualification: comparison to ConsistencyTTA (0.017 vs 0.013 RTF) shows more modest improvements; comparing to 200-step diffusion models inflates speedup numbers; missing direct 1-step vs 1-step comparisons with TangoFlux

Training efficiency analysis incomplete: two-stage training cost not compared to baselines; unclear how training time scales relative to competitors; partial data results (Table 2) show 464h without pretraining but efficiency gains not quantified

strengths: Achieves state-of-the-art single-step audio generation with 100x speedup (RTF 0.013), demonstrating significant practical value for deployment
Comprehensive evaluation including multiple objective metrics, human subjective evaluation with 10 professionals, and extensive ablation studies validating each component
Well-designed training methodology: instantaneous-to-mean curriculum with flow mix-up effectively addresses training instability and is convincingly validated through ablations
Clever integration of classifier-free guidance into training objective, eliminating runtime overhead while maintaining controllable generation
Compact model (120M parameters) trainable on consumer GPUs (~70 hours on 4 RTX 3090s), with efficient latent space modeling
Clear presentation with precise algorithms, informative architecture diagrams, and detailed experimental setup enabling reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited core methodological novelty: Mean Flows formulation from concurrent Geng et al. (2025), Flux-style architecture adapts existing designs (Esser et al. 2024), dual encoder is straightforward combination; primary novel contribution is the curriculum strategy which is incremental

Experimental comparison concerns: Table 1 mixes re-evaluated open-source with transcribed paper results creating inconsistency; comparisons use different training datasets; 100x speedup claim compares 1 NFE vs. 200 NFEs without per-NFE efficiency analysis

Training curriculum ablation (Table 3) confounds effects: FluxAudio trained on full dataset while MeanAudio-Scratch trained only on AudioCaps, making it difficult to isolate curriculum contribution from dataset effects
Heavy dependence on pre-trained components (FLAN-T5, CLAP, VAE, vocoder) and two-stage initialization from FluxAudio makes it difficult to isolate what is methodologically novel

Substantial acknowledged limitations: restricted to 10-second audio segments, cannot generate speech or handle fine-grained linguistic content, trained on 98% weakly-labeled data from LLMs/MLLMs with no analysis of label quality impact
Multi-step generation only competitive not superior: at 25 steps achieves FD=13.38 but TangoFlux achieves FD=20.65 at 50 steps; advantage primarily in efficiency not quality

Insufficient analysis of results: no error cases discussed, missing qualitative examples in main paper, limited investigation of why 75% flow mix-up ratio is optimal, Table 8 dual-encoder evaluation uses only 3 annotators on 10 samples

Theoretical justification gaps: Equation 3 (integrated CFG) lacks optimality justification and sensitivity analysis; Section 3.5 explanation of mean flow training failure is empirical not rigorous; Mean Flow Identity connection to single-step quality not intuitive

Evaluation concerns: metrics based on PANNs may not capture perceptual or linguistic fidelity; CLAP score has known limitations; human evaluation limited to 10 samples per configuration without inter-annotator agreement reporting

Code unavailable during review (only promised); complex two-stage pipeline makes exact reproduction difficult; relationship to concurrent flow-based approaches (FlashAudio, AudioTurbo) not deeply discussed

strengths: Strong empirical results on inference speed (0.013 RTF) with competitive generation quality (FD 14.30) compared to much larger models
Comprehensive and well-designed ablation studies (Tables 3-6) systematically evaluating training curriculum, flow mix-up, architectural components, and CFG scales
Practical efficiency: only 120M parameters, trainable on consumer-grade GPUs in ~70 hours, with promise to release code and weights
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (especially Figure 3) explaining the instantaneous-to-mean curriculum strategy
Well-motivated architectural choices including dual encoders (FLAN-T5 + CLAP) and integrated CFG that eliminates inference overhead
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: primarily applies existing MeanFlow framework (Geng et al., 2025) to audio generation; architectural components (MMDiT, DiT, ConvMLP, RoPE, SwiGLU) are standard; dual-encoder conditioning was used in prior TTA work

Weak theoretical justification for the key contribution (instantaneous-to-mean curriculum): explanation for training instability is vague, and the choice of 75% mixing ratio appears ad-hoc without principled justification or sensitivity analysis

Evaluation concerns: (1) unfair baseline comparisons using outdated models (2023-2024) with potentially smaller training datasets; (2) only 10 human experts evaluating 10 samples; (3) reliance on PANNs for metrics, which has known limitations; (4) '100x speedup' claim is misleading as it compares different step counts and architectures

Data quality issues inadequately addressed: only 49k/2.8M samples are human-annotated; majority rely on LLM-generated captions with no analysis of caption quality, potential biases, or impact on model performance; no ablation on weak vs. strong label proportions

Significant practical limitations underemphasized: hard 10-second audio limit; cannot handle speech or fine-grained linguistic content; unclear generalization beyond AudioCaps/MusicCaps; these severely restrict real-world applicability

Insufficient methodological details: hyperparameters (ω=0.3, κ=0.9) lack justification; no sensitivity analysis; curriculum scheduling not fully specified; dependency on FluxAudio initialization unexplored; unclear if method works from scratch at scale

Weak venue fit for ACL: this is fundamentally an audio/multimedia paper with standard off-the-shelf NLP components and no novel contributions to computational linguistics or text representation; better suited for ICASSP, Interspeech, or ICML

strengths: Impressive practical results: 100x speedup over existing diffusion-based TTA systems with RTF of 0.013, achieving single-step performance comparable to multi-step baselines while using only 120M parameters

Well-motivated instantaneous-to-mean curriculum with flow mix-up effectively addresses training instability through two-stage strategy combining standard flow matching pre-training and mixed-flow fine-tuning

Comprehensive evaluation including objective metrics (FAD, FD, KL, IS, CLAP), human ratings from audio professionals, extensive ablation studies covering architecture/training/flow configurations, and scalability analysis
Technical soundness with proper mathematical formulation, clear algorithms, strong reproducibility via detailed specifications, and commitment to code release

Well-designed architecture integrating multiple refinements (ConvMLP, RoPE, RMSNorm, SwiGLU) and complementary dual text encoders (FLAN-T5 + CLAP) that systematically improve generation quality and semantic alignment
Practical efficiency: 3-day training on 4x RTX 3090, avoids computational overhead of distillation methods, enables deployment on consumer hardware
Honest discussion of limitations (10-second restriction, weak label reliance, no speech) with transparent acknowledgment of generalization boundaries
weaknesses: Limited fundamental novelty: MeanFlow is concurrent work (Geng et al., 2025), Flux architecture adapted from prior art, training techniques established—main contribution is effective application rather than methodological innovation

Data quality concerns: Only ~2% of 2.8M samples (AudioCaps) have human annotations; remaining 2.75M use LLM/MLLM-generated captions with unquantified label noise. Impact on generalization not fully characterized despite authors acknowledging potential quality lag vs. proprietary models

Severely restricted audio scope: Fixed to 10-second generation with no handling of variable-length or long-form audio. This practically limits real-world applicability and represents an unaddressed technical limitation

Incomplete experimental rigor: Human evaluation with only 10 experts on 10 samples lacks confidence intervals and significance testing; flow mix-up ablation explores only 4 discrete points; CFG scale ablation limited to range 1-5 without justifying exploration boundaries

Insufficient mechanistic analysis: No explanation for why 75% flow mix-up is optimal; limited investigation of what mixed flows specifically improve over standard CFM; shallow architectural ablations that merely remove components without deeper analysis

Limited generalization scope: Evaluated only on general audio and music (no speech or specialized domains); English-only; out-of-distribution prompt behavior unexplored. Results may not generalize beyond AudioCaps-style descriptions
Marginal relevance to ACL: Fundamentally an audio processing paper with fixed text encoders—no NLP/computational linguistics contribution. Better suited for ICASSP/Interspeech venues

Incomplete analysis of design choices: Dual encoder contributions to different prompt types only briefly addressed in appendix; curriculum strategy benefits not isolated from components; multi-step generation trade-offs inadequately explored
